**Health:** The runner is running, every bot's books match the Alpaca paper account, no bots are stuck, and there were no errors.

**Fake money:** 73 live bots hold $72,654 together, down from $73,000 at the start. Bots running 24 hours ago lost $473 today (-0.7%), mostly because crypto fell. Stock galaxies were slightly up.

## Top and bottom bots

"Buy & Hold" means buying once and keeping it. Each bot is compared with its galaxy's Buy & Hold.

**Top 5 (all beat Buy & Hold):** Ethereum v3 · Daily Trend, v6 · 20-Day Breakout and v9 · Swing: 20-Day Breakout (0.0%, in cash, +3.7 points), Avalanche v2 · 20-Day Breakout (0.0%, +3.3), Ethereum v7 · Grid Bot (-1.7%, +2.0).

**Bottom 5 (all trail Buy & Hold):** Bitcoin v21 · 15-Min ICT Fair Value Gap (-4.4%, 2.8 points behind), and S&P 500 v2, v4, v6 and v7 (0.0%, 1.9 behind each). The S&P bots only trail because they waited in cash while stocks rose.

## Shadow league

Shadow bots follow live prices with pretend books and never place orders. EMA 12/26 trend and 20-day breakout each beat Buy & Hold on 10 of 39 assets; 90-day momentum, 200-day guard and daily trend on 9; golden cross on 6. Two days of data means nothing yet.

## Trades in the last 24 hours: 27

- The stock Buy & Hold bots bought their first shares at Friday's early close.
- Bitcoin v21 · ICT Fair Value Gap made 3 more quick trades, each a small loss: 12 trades, no wins, $28.61 in fees, as its backtest (a test on past prices) warned.
- Bitcoin v2 · Hourly Trend, v12 · 4-Hour MACD and the coin flip sold.
- Bitcoin v3 and v4 · 4-Hour Trend bought back in this morning.

## Lab notes

- The two queued ideas (swing breakout on every coin, "3 down days" swing on every stock fund) skipped their tests again because another heavy program was open. They'll run later.
- No bots added, promoted or retired. The oldest bot is 2 days old; the rules want 30+ days first.
- Scorecard: every strategy is "Too early". "Real-use candidate" needs 90+ days live, so none is close.

*Reminder: this is all fake money, and results from the first few months are mostly luck.*

overview.why: We want to find out which way of buying and selling works best, without risking any real money. So we gave a team of robots pretend money and let them race.
overview.kid: Each robot has its own rule for when to buy and when to sell. A couple of robots just buy and hold, so we can tell if the others are really smart or just lucky. Each galaxy is one thing they trade, like Bitcoin or Gold. Gold means doing fine, blue means making money, and red on fire means losing money.

BTC/USD.why: Bitcoin is the biggest cryptocurrency, so it's where we test the most ideas.
BTC/USD.kid: Bitcoin is digital money that no bank controls. Its price jumps around a lot, which makes it a good playground for robots.

ETH/USD.why: Ethereum is the second-biggest coin. Testing the same rules here shows if they only work on Bitcoin.
ETH/USD.kid: Ethereum is a digital coin that also runs little computer programs. It often moves like Bitcoin, but bigger.

SOL/USD.why: Solana is a faster, younger coin with bigger swings, a tougher test for every rule.
SOL/USD.kid: Solana is a newer digital coin. Newer coins can go up a lot, and down a lot.

XRP/USD.why: XRP is one of the oldest big coins, made for sending money between banks.
XRP/USD.kid: XRP is a digital coin built to move money across the world quickly.

DOGE/USD.why: Dogecoin is a 'meme coin' that started as a joke. It shows how wild crypto can be.
DOGE/USD.kid: Dogecoin has a dog on it and was made for fun. Its price moves on jokes and internet hype.

LINK/USD.why: Chainlink is a mid-sized coin, so we can see if rules work beyond the famous ones.
LINK/USD.kid: Chainlink is a coin that helps crypto programs learn about the real world, like prices and weather.

AVAX/USD.why: Avalanche is a smaller coin that has dropped a lot, a stress test for our rules.
AVAX/USD.kid: Avalanche is a digital coin that competes with Ethereum. Smaller coins can fall very far.

SPY.why: The S&P 500 is 'the stock market' most people mean. It's the main stock scorekeeper.
SPY.kid: SPY owns a tiny piece of the 500 biggest companies in America, all in one.

QQQ.why: The Nasdaq-100 is heavy on tech companies, so it's bumpier than the S&P 500.
QQQ.kid: QQQ owns pieces of the 100 biggest companies on the Nasdaq, like Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia.

DIA.why: The Dow is the oldest stock average in the news. Its swing bot tests buying short dips in 30 giant companies.
DIA.kid: DIA owns little pieces of the 30 big companies in the Dow Jones average, like Apple, Coca-Cola and Boeing.

IWM.why: Small companies often move differently from giant ones. This galaxy checks that.
IWM.kid: IWM owns little pieces of 2,000 smaller American companies.

GLD.why: Gold is what people buy when they're scared, so it often zigs when stocks zag.
GLD.kid: GLD owns real gold bars locked in a vault. You own a tiny slice of them.

TLT.why: Government bonds are the 'safe' part of most retirement plans. This galaxy shows how safe they are.
TLT.kid: TLT owns loans to the US government. The government pays interest, and the price moves when interest rates change.

NVDA.why: Nvidia makes the chips behind AI. One company can swing much more than a whole fund.
NVDA.kid: Nvidia makes the computer chips that power AI. It's one company, so it can soar or crash on its own.

AAPL.why: Apple is one of the biggest companies in the world, a steadier single stock.
AAPL.kid: Apple makes iPhones and Macs. Owning a share means owning a tiny bit of the company.

TSLA.why: Tesla is one of the bumpiest big stocks, a tough test for trading rules.
TSLA.kid: Tesla makes electric cars. Its price moves a lot on news and hype.

Coin Breakout Portfolio.why: In the lab's portfolio tests, one slow rule spread across many coins beat holding those coins with half the worst drop (+135% vs +34%, worst drop -34% vs -75%). This galaxy tests it live.
Coin Breakout Portfolio.kid: The $1,000 is split into 11 equal piggy banks, one per coin. Each follows the same rule: buy when its coin hits a 20-day high, sell when it hits a 10-day low. If a few coins crash, the others can carry it.

Swing Wide Portfolio.why: The swing rules (in and out within a week) spread over 27 assets, with equal money in each. In the lab's test it made about as much as holding the same assets with a quarter of the worst drop. It is the plain version the two swing pots are compared against.
Swing Wide Portfolio.kid: The $1,000 is split into 27 equal piggy banks, one per asset. Each waits for its own good moment, buys, and sells again within a week. A piggy bank never borrows from the others.

Swing Shared Pot.why: Same assets and swing rules as the Swing Wide Portfolio, but the cash is shared. Equal slices leave most money idle, because only a few assets have a setup at once. A shared pot puts more of it to work, which made more in the lab's test but with bigger drops.
Swing Shared Pot.kid: Everyone shares one big piggy bank. Whoever finds a good moment takes a tenth of it and puts the money back after selling, at most a week later. If ten are already out, the next one has to wait.

Swing Risk Pot.why: Same shared pot, but trades are sized by risk: a jumpy coin gets a small trade and a calm stock fund a bigger one, so no single trade can hurt much. It had the smoothest ride in the lab's test.
Swing Risk Pot.kid: Everyone shares one big piggy bank, but wild assets like Dogecoin only get a small handful and calm ones like the Dow get a bigger handful. That way one wild day can't spill much.

ideas.title: Breakout with a 200-day safety filter
ideas.why: Breakouts beat Buy & Hold on 4 of 5 assets in the 2-year test; a 200-day filter might avoid false breakouts in downtrends.
ideas.result: Passed on 10 of 33 assets (30%). Average vs Buy & Hold: +24%. Average robustness: 40%.

ideas.title: RSI bounce only in uptrends
ideas.why: Bounce rules failed in falling markets; buying dips only while above the 200-day average may fix that.
ideas.result: Passed on 9 of 33 assets (27%). Average vs Buy & Hold: -23%. Average robustness: 37%.

ideas.title: Daily trend with a 200-day safety filter
ideas.why: The daily 20/50 rule is the lab's best so far; adding the 200-day filter could cut losses in long downtrends.
ideas.result: Passed on 12 of 38 assets (32%). Average vs Buy & Hold: -17%. Average robustness: 38%.

ideas.title: Slow momentum (6 months)
ideas.why: Academic research (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen) found 12-month momentum worked in 58 of 58 markets; 6 months is a common shorter version.
ideas.result: Passed on 5 of 38 assets (13%). Average vs Buy & Hold: +10%. Average robustness: 29%.

ideas.title: RSI-2 dip on stock funds in uptrends
ideas.why: RSI-2 had a 7% chance of losing on the S&P 500 but trailed holding; the 200-day filter is how it is usually traded.
ideas.result: Passed on 1 of 21 assets (5%). Average vs Buy & Hold: -48%. Average robustness: 11%.

ideas.title: Slow momentum (12 months)
ideas.why: The research this came from (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen) used 12-month momentum; our 6-month test failed, so test the setting the research actually used. Uses 365 daily bars (12 months for coins, about 17 months of trading days for stock funds).
ideas.result: Passed on 7 of 38 assets (18%). Average vs Buy & Hold: -2%. Average robustness: 37%.

ideas.title: 20-day breakout with a slower exit (20-day low)
ideas.why: The 20-day breakout is the lab's strongest rule; selling at a 20-day low instead of a 10-day low should mean fewer whipsaw trades and fees, and let winners run longer.
ideas.result: Passed on 8 of 33 assets (24%). Average vs Buy & Hold: +10%. Average robustness: 42%.

ideas.title: Swing 20-day breakout (out within 7 days) on every coin
ideas.why: The swing desk's 20-day breakout with a 7-day limit was only tested on Bitcoin and Ethereum; one change from the breakout rule (sell after 7 days at the latest) tried on all coins shows whether the shorter hold holds up beyond those two.

ideas.title: Swing 3 down days (out within 5 days) on every stock fund
ideas.why: The 3-down-days swing setup did well on SPY in the swing test (Sharpe 1.02, worst drop -7%); trying the same setup on all stock funds checks whether it is a real pattern or one lucky fund.

bots.name: btc-hold
bots.description: Benchmark: buy $1,000 of Bitcoin once and hold
bots.plain: Bought $1,000 of Bitcoin on day one and never sells. Every other Bitcoin bot has to beat this to be worth anything.
bots.why: This robot is the scorekeeper. If another Bitcoin robot can't beat it, that robot isn't really being smart.
bots.kid: It bought Bitcoin once and just keeps it, like putting a toy in a box and never trading it away.
bots.title: Bitcoin v1 · Buy & Hold

plan.next: Never sells. It just holds, so other bots have something to beat.

bots.name: btc-1h-ma
bots.description: Original bot: 20 vs 50 hour averages
bots.plain: Checks every hour. Owns Bitcoin while the last 20 hours' average price is above the last 50 hours'. Trades a lot, so fees add up.
bots.why: It shows what happens when a robot trades a lot. Every trade costs a tiny fee, like paying a coin every time you swap cards.
bots.kid: Every hour it asks: lately, is the price higher than usual? If yes, it buys. If no, it sells. Like checking the sky every hour to decide if you need a jacket.
bots.title: Bitcoin v2 · Hourly Trend

plan.next: Buys when the 20-hour average rises above the 50-hour average (it's 1.17% below now).

bots.name: btc-4h-ma
bots.description: Trade less: 20 vs 50 four-hour averages
bots.plain: Same idea as the hourly bot, but looks at 4-hour chunks, so it trades less often.
bots.why: It tests whether checking less often works better than checking every hour.
bots.kid: It asks the same question as the hourly robot, but only every 4 hours, so tiny wiggles in the price don't fool it as much.
bots.title: Bitcoin v3 · 4-Hour Trend

plan.next: Sells when the 80-hour average drops below the 200-hour average. Safety net: sells if the price falls to $56,484.68 (5% below its buy).

bots.name: btc-4h-limit
bots.description: Same as btc-4h-ma but with cheaper limit orders
bots.plain: A twin of the 4-hour bot that uses limit orders (names its own price and waits) to pay lower fees.
bots.why: It tests whether being careful with fees makes a real difference.
bots.kid: It follows the exact same rule as its twin, but instead of paying whatever the price is, it says "I'll pay this much" and waits. That costs smaller fees.
bots.title: Bitcoin v4 · 4-Hour Trend, Low-Fee

plan.next: Sells when the 80-hour average drops below the 200-hour average. Safety net: sells if the price falls to $56,395.32 (5% below its buy).

bots.name: btc-4h-trend
bots.description: 4-hour averages, only when price is above its 200-day average
bots.plain: The 4-hour bot plus a safety filter: it only buys when Bitcoin is above its 200-day average (the long-term trend is up).
bots.why: It tests if a safety rule helps: only play when the big picture looks good.
bots.kid: Before doing anything, it checks the long-term trend: the average price over the last 200 days. If the price is below that, it stays out, like not going swimming when it's stormy.
bots.title: Bitcoin v5 · 4-Hour Trend + Safety Filter

plan.next: Waits until Bitcoin closes a day above $71,811.42, then buys when the 80-hour average rises above the 200-hour average (it's 0.15% above now).

bots.name: btc-regime
bots.description: Switches rules: own in uptrends, 4h averages when mixed, cash in downtrends
bots.plain: Changes its rule with the market's mood. Uptrend: just own Bitcoin. Mixed: use the 4-hour averages. Downtrend: sit in cash.
bots.why: It tests an idea real traders use: have a different plan for different kinds of market weather.
bots.kid: Sunny market (prices going up): it just holds Bitcoin. Cloudy (mixed): it uses the 4-hour rule. Stormy (prices going down): it hides in cash until the storm passes.
bots.title: Bitcoin v6 · Weather Switcher

plan.next: Mood is downtrend, so it stays in cash until Bitcoin closes a day above $71,811.42.

bots.name: btc-1d-ma
bots.description: Trade even less: 20 vs 50 day averages
bots.plain: Same idea again, but with daily prices: 20-day average vs 50-day average. Trades only a few times a year.
bots.why: It was the best Bitcoin robot in our 2-year test, so we want to see if that keeps happening for real.
bots.kid: It only looks once a day. It buys when prices have been rising for weeks and sells when they start falling. Slow and patient, like a turtle.
bots.title: Bitcoin v7 · Daily Trend

plan.next: Buys when the 20-day average rises above the 50-day average (it's 12.25% below now).

bots.name: btc-4h-rsi
bots.description: Buys Bitcoin after a sharp drop (RSI below 30, meaning 'oversold'), and sells once it bounces back (RSI above 55).
bots.plain: Buys Bitcoin after a sharp drop (RSI below 30, meaning 'oversold'), and sells once it bounces back (RSI above 55).
bots.why: It tests the opposite of trend bots: instead of following the crowd, it buys when everyone is panicking.
bots.kid: When the price falls really fast, like a ball dropped hard, it often bounces a little. This robot tries to catch the bounce.
bots.title: Bitcoin v8 · 4-Hour RSI Bounce

plan.next: Buys if RSI drops below 30, meaning Bitcoin fell hard (it's 42 now).

bots.name: btc-4h-bollinger
bots.description: Draws a 'normal range' around Bitcoin's average price. Buys when the price drops below the range and sells when it gets back to the middle.
bots.plain: Draws a 'normal range' around Bitcoin's average price. Buys when the price drops below the range and sells when it gets back to the middle.
bots.why: Another bounce strategy, so we can compare two ways of spotting a price that fell 'too far'.
bots.kid: Imagine a hallway the price usually walks in. When the price stumbles out the bottom, the robot buys, betting it walks back in.
bots.title: Bitcoin v9 · 4-Hour Bollinger Bounce

bots.plain: Buys when Bitcoin closes at its highest price in 20 days, and sells when it closes at its lowest in 10. A famous 1980s rule called 'Turtle Trading'.

bots.plain: Owns Bitcoin whenever it's worth more than it was 30 days ago.

bots.plain: Owns Bitcoin while its 50-day average is above its 200-day average. News sites call that crossing a 'golden cross'.

bots.plain: Buys $20 of Bitcoin every week no matter what, until its $1,000 is used up (about a year). Never sells.

bots.description: Flips a coin every day to decide whether to own Bitcoin. It has no plan, on purpose.
bots.plain: Flips a coin every day to decide whether to own Bitcoin. It has no plan, on purpose.

bots.kid: Heads it owns the coin, tails it doesn't. If a smart robot loses to this one, it isn't so smart.
bots.title: Bitcoin v16 · Coin Flip (Control)

bots.name: btc-ict-fvg
bots.description: An ICT-style bot on 15-minute candles. Buys only, because our account can't bet on prices falling.
